lessons.title: Preparing for shearing
lessons.html:
Planning the shearing

Shearing is the highest-income event of the year on a wool or mohair farm. A well-organised shed protects the value of the clip, keeps animals and people safe and keeps the shearing team working without delays. As supervisor you plan the dates, the team, the animals and the shed.

Weeks before shearing

  • Book the shearing team and classer and agree on dates, rates in ZAR and accommodation.
  • Plan the order of mobs: usually younger, finer animals such as lambs or kids first, then ewes, then rams, so that classes are not mixed and finer wool is not contaminated.
  • Order enough approved wool packs, fasteners, stencils and bale books.
  • Check the press, scales, wool tables, bins, handpieces and power supply.
  • Plan crutching or dagging beforehand so that dung-stained wool is removed.

Preparing the shed

  • Sweep and clean the board, pens, tables and bins. Remove all plastic, twine, feathers and rubbish.
  • Repair broken boards, grates and gates in the catching pens.
  • Ensure good lighting and ventilation.
  • Set out first aid kit, fire extinguisher and emergency numbers.

Preparing the animals

  • Bring animals in to the shed the day before so that they are dry. Wet wool must not be shorn or packed; keep enough animals under cover if rain threatens.
  • Hold animals off feed for some hours before shearing as the farm procedure states, so they are more comfortable and there is less dung on the board, but give access to water.
  • Do not shear heavily pregnant animals close to birth unless the manager and vet agree.

lessons.title: Running the shed on the day
lessons.html:
The shed team and their jobs

RoleJob
Penner-upKeeps catching pens full so shearers never wait
ShearersShear animals cleanly with minimal second cuts
Board hand / picker-upPicks up fleece, sweeps the board, keeps bellies and locks separate
Wool handlers / rollersThrow fleeces on the table and skirt them
ClasserClasses fleeces into lines according to industry standards
PresserPresses and marks bales, keeps the bale book

Workflow

  1. Animals flow from the pens to the catching pens, to the shearer, then out through the chute to the counting-out pen.
  2. Fleeces flow from the board to the table, to the classer's bins and to the press.
  3. Keep these two flows separate and smooth. A blockage anywhere slows the whole shed.

Quality control

  • Keep bellies, pieces, locks and crutchings separate from fleece.
  • Keep coloured and kemp-affected fleece separate.
  • Sweep the board after every animal.
  • No smoking, eating or plastic on the board or tables.
  • Check that each bale has only one line and is pressed to the correct weight.

Animal welfare

Shearers must handle animals firmly but gently. Cuts must be treated with a wound spray suitable for the purpose; serious cuts must be stitched or seen by the vet. After shearing, animals are vulnerable to cold. Keep freshly shorn animals in shelter if cold, wet or windy weather is forecast, and give them feed. Count every pen out and record the tally per shearer.

lessons.title: Safety, records and dispatch
lessons.html:
Safety in the shed

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 applies in the shearing shed.

  • Electrical: check cables, plugs and handpieces before the day. Use an earth leakage unit. Never work on a machine that is switched on.
  • Handpieces: a handpiece that locks up can spin and cut. Shearers must disengage the drive before putting it down.
  • Back injuries: rotate jobs where possible, provide back supports and allow rest breaks.
  • Wool press: only trained people operate it; keep hands and heads clear when it moves.
  • Slips and trips: keep the board and walkways dry and clear.
  • Fire: wool and dust burn. No smoking in or near the shed; keep extinguishers ready.
  • Hygiene: provide clean water, toilets and hand washing. Treat cuts to people quickly.

Records

  • Shearer tally: number of animals shorn per shearer per day for payment.
  • Bale book / specification: bale number, line, mass and description for each bale.
  • Mob records: which mob was shorn, numbers, dates.
  • Incident register: injuries to people or animals.

Dispatch

Mark each bale clearly with the farm brand, the line and the bale number. Store bales dry on pallets, away from fuel and chemicals, and in a locked store. Arrange transport to the broker, and send the bale specification with the load. Check the count and get the transporter to sign for the bales.

After shearing

Clean the shed, service handpieces and press, list repairs, and review what went well and what caused delays.

Key points

  • Plan team, dates, packs and mob order well before shearing.
  • Shear only dry animals and keep the shed free of plastic and rubbish.
  • Keep animal flow and fleece flow separate and smooth.
  • Protect freshly shorn animals from cold weather.
  • Control electrical, press and back injury hazards.
  • Keep accurate tallies and bale records and dispatch bales securely.

quiz.question: Which job keeps the catching pens full so shearers do not wait?
Why are animals brought under cover the day before shearing?

options.text: So that they are dry, because wet wool must not be shorn or packed
So that they can be dipped
So that they can be vaccinated

quiz.question: Freshly shorn sheep face cold, wet weather. What should you do?

options.text: Turn them out on the open veld immediately
Keep them in shelter and give them feed

quiz.question: What is the shearer tally used for?

options.text: Recording animals shorn per shearer for payment

quiz.question: Which mob is usually shorn first?

options.text: Younger, finer animals such as lambs or kids

quiz.question: A bale may contain several different lines of wool if it is pressed well.
An earth leakage unit should be used with shearing machines.
Which actions protect the quality of the clip? (select all that apply)

options.text: Sweep the board after every animal
Keep bellies and locks separate from fleece
Use plastic feed bags as wool packs
Remove plastic and twine from the shed
Allow eating on the wool tables
